course.title: Geometry: Shape and Space
course.description: Turn, cut, scale and unfold. Discover how shapes measure the world around you.
course.audience: An adult comfortable with arithmetic, fractions and basic algebra. No previous geometry course is assumed.

paragraphs: Geometry is the part of mathematics that measures shape and space: how much turn there is in a corner, how far it is round a field, how many tiles a floor needs and how large a box must be to hold what goes in it. The word comes from the Greek for measuring the earth, and the subject has kept that practical character, since every plan, map and package carries lengths, angles and areas that have to come out right.

The measurements of a shape are tied together by fixed rules, so that a few known ones settle the rest. The three angles of a triangle always make up the same amount of turn, which means that two of them determine the third. A right triangle's three sides are linked by a single equation, so any two of them give the third and a distance can be found without being measured. When a shape is enlarged, its lengths, areas and volumes grow by different amounts, which is why a box twice as long in every direction holds eight times as much.

Several of these rules were proved by Euclid in the Elements, about 300 BCE, and each can still be tested against a drawing, so you can see why a rule holds as well as how to use it. With the right rule, a missing angle, the area of a floor or the height of a tower can be found from measurements that are easy to take.
outcomes: You'll be able to find a missing angle in a corner, on a straight line, round a point and inside a triangle.
You'll be able to tell the distance round a shape from the space inside it, and work out both for rectangles.
You'll be able to find the area of a triangle, a parallelogram, a trapezoid and a shape with a corner cut away.
You'll be able to say how a shape's lengths, areas and volumes change when it is enlarged.
You'll be able to find the distance between two points on a grid and the volume and surface area of a box.

lessons.title: Measuring turns

lead.text: The figure shows a room from above, with the door in the top wall and a dashed line pointing at it. Turn until you face the right-hand wall and you have made a **quarter-turn**; turn on until your back is to the door and you have made a **half-turn**, which is two quarter-turns; and turn all the way back to the door and you have made a **whole turn**, which is four.

afterFigure.text: Nothing in this counting depends on the size of the room, because a turn is a fraction of the way round and not a distance. A half-turn is always *worth two* quarter-turns, and **four quarter-turns always make a whole turn**, so any turn built from quarters can be followed simply by counting them.

diagram.caption: The dashed line points at the door, the curved arrow shows the turn and the solid line shows the way you end up facing. Use the buttons to compare the three.

lead.text: Quarter-turns are enough for a turn that ends at a wall, but most turns end somewhere in between, so a whole turn is divided into 360 equal parts and each part is called a **degree**, written 1°.

afterFigure.text: Since a whole turn is 360°, a half-turn is *half* of that, 180°, and a quarter-turn is a *quarter* of it. The number 360 is generally traced to Babylonian astronomers, whose number system counted in sixties, and it has lasted because it divides exactly by every whole number from 1 to 10 except 7, so that most simple fractions of a turn come out as whole degrees.

The amount of turn between two straight lines that start at the same point is called an **angle**, and the two lines are its **arms**. An angle that is a quarter of a whole turn is a **right angle**, the square corner of a page or a door frame, and a diagram marks it with a small square.

diagram.caption: Each wedge is drawn to scale, measured round from the horizontal arm. Use the buttons to compare the sizes.

lead.text: A right angle is a quarter of a whole turn, 90°, and a line drawn out of the corner splits it into two smaller angles. Together they still fill the corner, so **the two angles add up to 90°**.

afterFigure.text: That makes the unknown part the *difference* between 90° and the known one. If the marked part is 25°, the rest is 90° − 25° = 65°.

lead.text: A straight line is a half-turn: stand facing along it, turn until you face the opposite way, and you have turned through 180°. A line drawn up from any point on it makes two angles that sit side by side, and since together they take up the half-turn, **they add up to 180°**. The half-turn between the two ends of the line is called a **straight angle**.

afterFigure.text: If the given angle is 120°, the other is 180° − 120° = 60°. The total is now 180° instead of 90°, but the *method* has not changed: subtract the part you know from the whole.

lead.text: When several lines meet at a single point, the angles between them go all the way round, and the full circuit is a whole turn, so **the angles round a point add up to 360°**.

afterFigure.text: The figure shows 200° of the turn made and the rest still to come. The two together make 360°, so the rest is 360° − 200° = 160°. A point with three or more angles round it works the same way: add up the angles you know and take the sum from 360°.

The three totals are one idea. A corner holds a quarter-turn, a straight line a half-turn and a point a whole turn, which are 90°, 180° and 360°, and in each case the unknown angle is *what the known angles leave over*.

lead.text: Draw the two arms of an angle longer and nothing about the turn between them changes.

afterFigure.text: A degree measures how far one arm has turned from the other, not how far the arms reach across the page, so **an angle is fixed by the turn between its arms**. Drawing an angle larger makes the picture bigger and leaves the angle as it was, which is why an angle whose arms are too short to reach the scale of a protractor can have them extended before it is measured.

diagram.alt: Two angles side by side, one with long arms and one with short arms. Both are right angles of 90 degrees.
diagram.caption: Both angles are the same size. Only the directions of the arms set the turn, so the longer arms add nothing.

blocks.text: Stand facing a wall and turn until it is directly on your right, then keep turning until it is behind you, and you have made two turns of the same size, each a quarter of the way round. The corner of a page, the edge of a ruler and the meeting point of the spokes of a wheel all hold turns of this kind, and geometry measures each of them in the same way, as **an amount of turn**, a fraction of the way round a full circle.

The fractions are fixed: the corner of the page is always the same amount of turn, and so is the straight edge, and so is the whole way round the hub. That is what makes an angle findable without a protractor, because when part of a fixed amount is known, the rest is whatever is left over.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to find an unknown angle in a corner, on a straight line and round a point.

recap.keyIdea: An angle measures an amount of turn, so the angles in a corner add up to 90°, along a straight line to 180° and round a point to 360°.

blocks.text: A whole turn is 360°, which makes a half-turn 180° and a quarter-turn, the [[right angle|An angle that is a quarter of a whole turn, 90°. Met earlier in this lesson.]], 90°, and an angle measures how far one arm has turned from the other, whatever the length of the arms.
To find an unknown angle, decide whether the angles fill a corner, a line or a point, take the matching total of 90°, 180° or 360°, and subtract the angles you already know.

recap.nextHook: A triangle has three corners, and the turns at those corners also add up to a fixed total, which the next lesson uses to find a missing angle.

lessons.title: Angles in triangles

lead.text: The figure shows two triangles with their three angles marked, and when you add each set the total is the same: 35° + 105° + 40° = 180° for the first, and 80° + 25° + 75° = 180° for the second.

afterFigure.text: Laid side by side, the three corners fill a straight line, which is a [[half-turn|Half of a whole turn, 180°. Met in “Measuring turns”.]] of 180°, so **the three angles of every triangle add up to 180°**. Euclid proved the result in Book I of his *Elements*, about 300 BCE, by drawing a line through one corner parallel to the opposite side, which cuts the straight line at that corner into the same three angles. The proof shows that the total belongs to every triangle, and not only to the ones that have been measured.

lead.text: Because the three angles fill 180°, a missing one is whatever the other two *leave*.

afterFigure.text: The two known angles use up 62° + 41° = 103° of the line, so the third angle is 180° − 103° = 77°. Taking the angles away one at a time, 180° − 62° − 41°, gives the same 77°, since subtracting a sum is the same as subtracting its parts. Either way **the missing angle is 180° minus the angles you know**, and adding all three angles back is a quick check that they come to 180°.

diagram.alt: A triangle with two corners of 62 and 41 degrees, and under it a straight line of 180 degrees split into the same two angles. The first view leaves the third corner unknown, and the second shows it is 77 degrees.
diagram.caption: The two known corners use up 103° of the straight line. What is left is the third corner.

lead.text: A triangle with one right angle is called a **right triangle**, and its other two angles are each *smaller* than 90°, which makes them **acute** angles. The right angle takes 90° of the 180° available, so the two acute angles have 180° − 90° = 90° between them.

afterFigure.text: The figure shows two examples. In the first, 90° and 20° leave 180° − 90° − 20° = 70° for the third angle, and in the second, 90° and 65° leave 25°. In both the two acute angles add to 90°, which means that **in a right triangle one acute angle fixes the other**: subtract it from 90°.

lead.text: A triangle can have two sides of equal length, and it is then called an **isosceles** triangle. The angles opposite those two sides are equal as well, so an isosceles triangle has a pair of equal angles and a third angle that *differs* from them.

afterFigure.text: The equal pair share whatever the odd angle leaves of the 180°. If the odd angle is 40°, the other two share 180° − 40° = 140° and each is 140° ÷ 2 = 70°.

steps.headline: When three angles make a triangle

lead.text: The total of 180° also tells you whether three angles can belong to a triangle at all. Lay the angles end to end along a straight line of 180° and see what happens.

afterFigure.text: The set 30°, 60° and 90° fills the line exactly, so those angles can be the corners of a triangle. The set 50°, 60° and 80° totals 190° and runs 10° past the end, and 40°, 60° and 70° totals 170° and leaves a gap of 10°, so neither set can. A triangle therefore needs **three positive angles that add to exactly 180°**, and *any other* total fails.

diagram.alt: Three sets of angles laid end to end along a straight line of 180 degrees. 30, 60 and 90 fill it exactly, 50, 60 and 80 run past the end, and 40, 60 and 70 leave a gap.
diagram.caption: Lay the three angles end to end along the line. Only when they fill it exactly can they be the corners of a triangle.

blocks.text: The three corners torn from a paper triangle fit together along a straight edge, with their points touching and no gap or overlap, whether the triangle was tall and narrow, short and wide or lopsided.

A straight edge is a [[half-turn|Half of a whole turn, 180°. Met in “Measuring turns”.]], so the fit says something exact about how much turn three corners hold between them, and that one fact lets you find a corner of any triangle without measuring it.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to find a missing angle of a triangle and decide whether three angles can belong to one.

recap.keyIdea: The three angles of a triangle always add up to 180°, so any one of them is 180° minus the other two.

blocks.text: The three corners of a triangle laid side by side fill a straight line, which is why their angles add up to 180° whatever the shape, a result Euclid proved in Book I of the *Elements*. A missing angle is therefore 180° minus the angles you know; in a right triangle the two acute angles share 90°, and in an isosceles triangle the equal pair share what the odd angle leaves.
The same total tells you whether three angles could belong to a triangle: they must be positive and add to exactly 180°.

lessons.title: Boundary and area

lead.text: To say how much surface a shape covers, we cover it with **unit squares**, squares whose sides are one unit long, and count them. The figure shows a rectangle 8 units long and 5 units wide, and the *Show unit squares* button draws the squares on it.

afterFigure.text: The first rectangle has 5 rows with 8 squares in each, so it holds 5 × 8 = 40 unit squares. The count is the **area** of the shape, measured in *square units*, and because every row of a rectangle has the same number of squares, **the area of a rectangle is its length multiplied by its width**.

lead.text: Skirting board is measured the *other* way, by walking round the edge of a room and adding up the lengths of the walls. The total distance round the edge of a shape is called its **perimeter**, and the figure shows two rooms whose walls come in two equal pairs.

afterFigure.text: Opposite sides of a rectangle are equal, so going round the edge means length + width + length + width, which is 2 × (length + width). For the first room that is 9 + 4 + 9 + 4 = 26 units. **A perimeter is a distance, so it is measured in ordinary units of length**, such as metres or centimetres.

steps.headline: The perimeter and the area of a 6 by 4 rectangle

workedSteps.text: Add the four sides of the rectangle to find its perimeter.
Now count the unit squares inside it, row by row, to find its area.

lead.text: A fence of a fixed length can be laid out in many shapes, so one perimeter does not settle the area. Both rooms in the figure have the *same* perimeter of 16 units, yet the first is a 4 by 4 square and the second is a long strip 7 by 1.

afterFigure.text: The square covers 4 × 4 = 16 unit squares, while the strip covers only 7 × 1 = 7, so with the same boundary one room has more than twice the floor of the other. The reverse also holds, since a 4 by 4 square and an 8 by 2 rectangle both cover 16 square units but have perimeters of 16 and 20 units. **Perimeter and area are separate measurements**, and neither can be found from the other alone.

lead.text: The same room, 8 metres by 3 metres, can now be measured both ways, as the figure shows. Along the edge the walls add up to 8 + 3 + 8 + 3 = 22 metres, which is the length of skirting board, fence or frame it needs. Across the inside, 3 rows of 8 squares give 8 × 3 = 24 squares, which is how much tile, turf or paint it needs.

afterFigure.text: The units show which measurement you have. A perimeter is a length and is written in metres, but an area counts squares one metre on each side, which are *square metres*, written m². **A number of square units says how much surface, and a number of plain units says how far round**.

lead.text: Sometimes the area is known and a side is missing. A floor is 5 tiles wide and takes 40 tiles in all.

afterFigure.text: The area is one side multiplied by the other, so 40 = 5 × (the other side), and since division *undoes* multiplication the other side is 40 ÷ 5 = 8 tiles. **Dividing the area by the side you know gives the side you do not**, and multiplying back, 8 × 5 = 40, checks the result.

blocks.text: A room 8 metres long and 3 metres wide needs two quite different kinds of material. Skirting board runs along the foot of the walls and is sold by the metre, while floor tiles cover the whole surface and are sold by the square metre, so one room gives rise to two separate measurements, one taken round its edge and one taken across its inside.
Both are worked out from the same two lengths and both come out as numbers, which is why they are so easily confused. They are different quantities, however, with different units and different uses.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to tell the distance round a rectangle from the space inside it, and work out both.

recap.keyIdea: Perimeter is the distance round a shape, in units of length, and area is the number of unit squares inside it, in square units.

blocks.text: A rectangle's perimeter adds its four sides, so it is 2 × (length + width) and is measured in plain units, while its area counts the unit squares inside it, so it is length × width and is measured in square units.

The two are independent: shapes with the same perimeter can enclose very different areas, which is why a problem has to say which one it wants. When the area and one side are known, dividing the area by that side gives the other.

recap.nextHook: Rectangles are the easy case, because every row has the same length; the next lesson finds the area of a triangle by relating it to a rectangle.

lessons.title: Base and height

lead.text: Cut a rectangular card along a diagonal and the two pieces are triangles that fit exactly over one another when one is turned through a [[half-turn|Half of a whole turn, 180°. Met in “Measuring turns”.]], so each piece is *half* of the card. The figure shows a card 10 units long and 3 units wide cut in this way.

afterFigure.text: The card has area 10 × 3 = 30 square units, and the two triangles share it equally, so each has area 30 ÷ 2 = 15 square units. The side a triangle stands on is called its **base**, and here that is the long side of 10 units, with the triangle rising 3 units above it.

steps.headline: The height of a leaning triangle

lead.text: The figure shows two triangles with the same base of 8 units, one with its top corner above the end of the base and one with it above the middle.

afterFigure.text: In both, the top corner is 6 units above the base, measured along a line that meets the base at a right angle, and that distance is the triangle's **perpendicular height**, usually shortened to its height. A sloping side is *not* the height, because it leans and so is longer than the straight drop, and **the height always meets the base at a right angle**. With the base drawn at the bottom, the height is simply the vertical distance from the top corner down to the base.

lead.text: The rectangle drawn round a triangle, with the same base and the same height, gives the area of any triangle. A line down from the top corner splits that rectangle into two smaller ones, and a side of the triangle cuts each of those exactly in half, so the triangle fills half of each part and therefore half of the whole rectangle. The *Show enclosing rectangle* button draws it.

afterFigure.text: The rectangle has area base × height, so **the area of any triangle is its base multiplied by its height, divided by 2**. In the figure the base is 12 units and the height 3, so the rectangle has area 12 × 3 = 36 and the triangle has area 18 square units, whether its corner leans left or right, because only the base and the height enter the calculation.

lead.text: A four-sided shape whose opposite sides are parallel is a **parallelogram**. A rectangle is one, and so is the leaning shape in the figure. A line drawn between two opposite corners cuts a parallelogram into two triangles that fit exactly over one another when one is turned through a half-turn.

afterFigure.text: Each of those triangles has the parallelogram's base and its perpendicular height, so each has area base × height ÷ 2, and together they have area base × height. **The area of a parallelogram is its base multiplied by its perpendicular height**, with no halving, and the lean makes no difference.

lead.text: The rule for a triangle can be run backwards when the area is known and the height is not. The triangle in the figure has a base of 6 centimetres and an area of 24 square centimetres.

afterFigure.text: Base × height ÷ 2 gives the area, so base × height is *twice* the area, which is 2 × 24 = 48. Dividing by the base then leaves the height, 48 ÷ 6 = 8 cm. **Double the area, then divide by the base**, and check by putting the height back in, since 6 × 8 ÷ 2 = 24.

diagram.alt: A triangle with a base of 6 centimetres and an area of 24 square centimetres. The first view marks its height as unknown. The second doubles the area to 48 and divides by 6 to get a height of 8 centimetres.
diagram.caption: Work backwards from the area: double it, then divide by the base.

blocks.text: The area of any triangle is half the area of the rectangle that has the same base and the same height, so two measurements are enough to find it.

The same relation holds for triangles of every shape, and it carries over to parallelograms. It needs the length of one side, called the base, and the height above it, which is measured at a right angle to the base and so does not always lie along an edge of the shape.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to find the area of a triangle or a parallelogram from its base and perpendicular height.

recap.keyIdea: A triangle's area is its base times its perpendicular height divided by 2, and a parallelogram's is its base times its perpendicular height.

blocks.text: Every triangle fills half of the rectangle that has its base and its height, so its area is base × height ÷ 2, where the height is the distance from the top corner to the base measured at a right angle. A parallelogram is two such triangles, so its area is base × height with no halving.

Because the rule uses only the base and the height, sliding the top corner sideways leaves the area unchanged, and the rule can be run backwards: double the area and divide by the base to find the height.

recap.nextHook: Many shapes are a combination of rectangles and triangles, and the next lesson finds their areas by adding pieces together or taking a missing corner away.

lessons.title: Pieces and cutouts

lead.text: A shape made by joining or cutting simple shapes is called a **composite shape**, and the commonest case is a rectangle with a corner taken out. The figure shows a rectangle 8 units long and 5 wide with a smaller rectangle removed from one corner, and the removed part is the **cutout**.

afterFigure.text: The floor that remains is the whole rectangle *less* the cutout. In the first view the whole rectangle covers 8 × 5 = 40 square units and the cutout covers 3 × 2 = 6, so the remaining shape covers 40 − 6 = 34 square units. **Find the area of the whole rectangle, then subtract the area of the cutout**.

lead.text: A [[composite shape|A shape made by joining or cutting simple shapes. Met earlier in this lesson.]] can also be measured by cutting it into pieces. The L-shaped floor in the figure is cut with one straight line into two rectangles, a 3 by 4 piece at the top and a 7 by 3 piece along the bottom, and the pieces do not overlap.

afterFigure.text: Their areas are 3 × 4 = 12 and 7 × 3 = 21 square metres, which add to 33 square metres. The second view reaches the same floor by the other route, a 7 by 7 square of 49 square metres less a 4 by 4 cutout of 16, and 49 − 16 = 33. Pieces that are added must not overlap, because a region lying in both would be counted *twice*.

lead.text: A four-sided shape with *one* pair of parallel sides is a **trapezoid**, called a trapezium in British usage, and its parallel sides are its **bases**. To measure one, take a second copy, turn it through a half-turn and fit it against the first along a slanted side, and the two together make a [[parallelogram|A four-sided shape whose opposite sides are parallel. Met in “Base and height”.]], a shape whose area you already know.

afterFigure.text: The parallelogram's base is the two bases laid end to end, 9 + 5 = 14 units in the first view, and its height is the trapezoid's height of 4, so its area is 14 × 4 = 56 and one trapezoid, which is half of it, has area 28 square units.

lead.text: Halving the parallelogram gives the rule for a trapezoid. If its bases are a and b and its height is h, the parallelogram has area (a + b) × h, so the trapezoid has *half* of that.

afterFigure.text: The rule can be read as the average of the two bases, (a + b) ÷ 2, multiplied by the height. In the figure the bases are 9 and 5 and the height is 4. The line halfway up is 7 long, the average of 9 and 5, and a rectangle 7 wide and 4 high covers 28 square centimetres, the same as the trapezoid, because **what the long base has in excess the short one lacks**.

blocks.text: A floor shaped like the letter L has no area formula of its own, yet its area is easy to find, because the L is built from rectangles and the area of a rectangle is its length multiplied by its width. There are two ways to use that: cut the L into two rectangles and add their areas, or complete it to one large rectangle and take away the corner that was missing.
Both rest on the same move, which is to replace a shape that has no rule of its own by shapes that do, and to combine their areas by adding or subtracting.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to find the area of a shape made from rectangles, and of a trapezoid.

recap.keyIdea: A composite shape is measured by adding pieces that do not overlap or by subtracting a cutout from the whole, and a trapezoid's area is the average of its bases times its height.

blocks.text: A shape with no rule of its own can be split into rectangles and added, or completed to a rectangle and reduced by the area of the missing corner. Both routes give the same area, and pieces that are added must not overlap.
Two copies of a trapezoid make a parallelogram whose base is the sum of the trapezoid's two bases, so one trapezoid has area (a + b) × h ÷ 2, the average of the bases multiplied by the height.

recap.nextHook: Not every shape has straight edges, and the next lesson turns to the circle, whose circumference and area both depend on its radius.

lessons.title: Around and inside circles

lead.text: Every point on the edge of a circle is the same distance from a point inside it, the **centre**, and that distance is the circle's **radius**. A straight line from one side of the circle to the other through the centre is a **diameter**. The figure shows two circles with their radius marked, and the *Show diameter* button adds the diameter.

afterFigure.text: A diameter is made of two radii placed end to end, one on each side of the centre, so a circle of radius 9 units has a diameter of 18. **The diameter is always twice the radius**, and the radius is *half* the diameter, so either one gives you the other.

lead.text: The distance all the way round a circle, which is its [[perimeter|The distance round the edge of a shape. Met in “Boundary and area”.]], is called its **circumference**. It is a curved length, so it cannot be found by adding up straight sides, but it can be compared with the diameter.

afterFigure.text: Three diameters fit along the rim with a short piece left over, about 0.14 of a diameter, and the same holds for every circle: **the circumference is always about 3.14 times the diameter**. That fixed ratio is the number **pi**, written π, whose decimal never ends or repeats, so 3.14 is a convenient approximation and not its exact value.

lead.text: Since the diameter is *two* radii, the rule for the circumference can be written with the radius, as 2 × π × r.

afterFigure.text: For a circle of radius 7 units the circumference is 2 × 3.14 × 7 = 43.96 units. Two steps are involved, the doubling that turns the radius into the diameter and the multiplication by π, and **forgetting the doubling is the usual way to go wrong**, because π × 7 is only the distance round half the circle.

lead.text: The boundary is a length and so involves a length once, but an area involves a length twice, once in each direction, as the area of a square does.

afterFigure.text: The circle covers about 3.14 of the squares that have the radius as their side, so **the area of a circle is π × r × r**. For a radius of 6 units that is 3.14 × 6 × 6 = 3.14 × 36 = 113.04 square units. Archimedes proved the rule in his *Measurement of a Circle* by showing that a circle has the same area as a right triangle whose base is its circumference and whose height is its radius, since ½ × 2πr × r = πr².

lead.text: The circumference rule can use the diameter directly, but the area rule needs the *radius*. A circle 14 centimetres across has a diameter of 14, so its circumference is 3.14 × 14 = 43.96 cm with no further step.

afterFigure.text: For the area the 14 must first be halved, giving a radius of 7 cm and an area of 3.14 × 7 × 7 = 3.14 × 49 = 153.86 cm². Squaring the diameter by mistake would give 3.14 × 14 × 14 = 615.44 cm², which is four times too large. **Halve the diameter before you square.**

lead.text: The two rules treat the radius differently, and that decides how a circle changes when it is enlarged. The circumference, 2πr, contains the radius *once*, while the area, πr², contains it *twice*.

afterFigure.text: Suppose the radius of the 14 cm circle is tripled, from 7 cm to 21 cm. The circumference becomes 2 × 3.14 × 21 = 131.88 cm, which is 3 times the 43.96 cm it was, whereas the area becomes 3.14 × 21 × 21 = 3.14 × 441 = 1384.74 cm², which is 9 times the 153.86 cm² it was. **A length grows by the same factor as the radius, but an area grows by that factor squared**.

lessons.orientation: Use radius and diameter correctly in circumference and circle-area calculations.

blocks.text: The distance all the way round a circle is a little more than three times the distance straight across it, through the middle. String laid round the rim of a plate and then straightened against its width shows this, and the ratio is the same for a coin or a running track, so it belongs to every circle, whatever its size.

A second fixed relation connects a circle's area to the distance from its middle to its edge, and the two together are enough to measure any circle, provided you keep track of which of two lengths a problem has given you.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to find the circumference and the area of a circle from its radius or its diameter.

recap.keyIdea: A circle's circumference is π times its diameter, or 2πr, and its area is π times the radius squared.

blocks.text: The diameter is twice the radius, and the distance round a circle is π times the diameter, or 2 × π × r, with π taken as 3.14. The space inside is π × r × r, which needs the radius itself, so a diameter must be halved before it is squared.
Because the circumference contains the radius once and the area contains it twice, enlarging a circle multiplies its circumference by the factor and its area by the factor squared.

recap.nextHook: Enlarging a shape changes its lengths and areas in different ways, and the next lesson begins with what it means for one shape to be an enlargement of another.

lessons.title: Same shape, new size

lead.text: Two shapes that have the same shape but not the same size are called **similar**. One is an enlargement or a reduction of the other, and every length in it is the matching length in the original multiplied by the *same* number, which is called the **scale factor**.

afterFigure.text: With a scale factor of 2 the width becomes 5 × 2 = 10 and the height 4 × 2 = 8. Because every length is multiplied by the same number, **the copy has the same shape as the original**: its corners are still [[right angles|An angle that is a quarter of a whole turn, 90°. Met in “Measuring turns”.]], and its height is still four fifths of its width.

lead.text: What matters is that the lengths are *multiplied*. Take a rectangle 3 units wide and 6 units tall, whose height is twice its width. Doubling both lengths gives 6 by 12, and the height is still twice the width, so the shape is unchanged.

afterFigure.text: Adding the same amount to both lengths does not work. Adding 3 to each gives 6 by 9, whose height is only one and a half times its width, and the rectangle is visibly fatter than before. Stretching one length alone fails for the same reason. **Only multiplying every length by one factor keeps the proportions**, which is why the rule for similar shapes says multiply and never add.

lead.text: To compare a shape with its copy, pair up the sides that sit in the *same* place. These are called **corresponding** sides: the shortest side of one with the shortest side of the other, the longest with the longest. Each pair differs by the scale factor, so the factor is found by dividing a length in the copy by the corresponding length in the original.

afterFigure.text: In the figure the small triangle has sides of 2, 3 and 4 centimetres, and a similar triangle has a shortest side of 6 centimetres. The shortest sides correspond, so the scale factor is 6 ÷ 2 = 3, and the other two sides of the larger triangle are 3 × 3 = 9 and 4 × 3 = 12 centimetres. **One pair of corresponding sides fixes the factor, and the factor then gives every other side.**

A stick 2 metres tall that casts a shadow 3 metres long forms a small triangle with the sun's ray, and a tower beside it that casts a shadow of 60 metres forms a larger triangle of the same shape, with a scale factor of 60 ÷ 3 = 20, so the tower is 2 × 20 = 40 metres tall.

lead.text: A scale factor less than 1 gives a *smaller* copy, and the multiplication works in just the same way: with a factor of 0.25, a length of 12 becomes 12 × 0.25 = 3.

afterFigure.text: A plan or a map is a **scale drawing**, a similar copy of the real thing, and its scale states the factor between the two. If 1 cm on a plan represents 50 cm in reality, every real length is 50 times its length on the plan, so a wall drawn 8 cm long is 8 × 50 = 400 cm long, which is 4 m once the centimetres are converted. **Multiply by the scale to go from the drawing to the real thing, divide by it to go back**, and convert the units at the end.

lessons.orientation: Match corresponding lengths and apply one scale factor to every dimension.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A photocopier set to 150% makes every length in the picture half as long again, the width and the height alike, so the copy is recognisably the same picture, only larger. A machine that stretched only the width would make faces come out wide and distorted, although the copy would be just as big.
What makes the copy look right is that a single number multiplies every length, which means that once you know how one length has changed you can work out how every other length has changed.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to find a scale factor from one pair of matching lengths and use it on every other length of a similar shape.

recap.keyIdea: Similar shapes have every length multiplied by the same scale factor, which is found by dividing a length in the copy by the corresponding length in the original.

blocks.text: A copy is similar to the original when one scale factor multiplies every length, which is why adding the same amount, or changing one length alone, changes the shape. The factor is the new length divided by the corresponding old length, and it applies to every other length.
A factor above 1 enlarges and a factor below 1 reduces, and a scale drawing is a reduction whose scale gives the factor between the drawing and the real thing.

recap.nextHook: A scale factor multiplies lengths, but areas respond to it differently, and the next lesson shows by how much.

lessons.title: When area scales

lead.text: Take a square tile 2 cm on each side, which has an area of 2 × 2 = 4 cm², and enlarge it with a [[scale factor|The number that multiplies every length in a similar copy. Met in “Same shape, new size”.]] of 6. Every side becomes 6 × 2 = 12 cm and the area becomes 12 × 12 = 144 cm².

afterFigure.text: To see what has happened to the area, count the copies of the original that cover the enlarged square. Six fit along each side and there are six rows of them, so the big square holds 6 × 6 = 36 small ones, which agrees with 144 ÷ 4 = 36. **The scale factor acts once along the width and once along the height**, so the area is multiplied by it *twice* over and not once.

lead.text: The result is not special to squares. A rectangle 4 units wide and 5 units tall has area 4 × 5 = 20 square units, and when both lengths are multiplied by a scale factor *k* the new width is k × 4 and the new height is k × 5, so the new area is (k × 4) × (k × 5) = k × k × 20. The number that multiplies the area, k × k, is called the **area factor**.

afterFigure.text: With k = 6 the area factor is 6 × 6 = 36 and the area is 36 × 20 = 720 square units, while k = 8 gives an area factor of 64 and an area of 1280. **The area factor is the square of the length scale factor**, written k², and it holds for every shape, straight-edged or curved, because any shape can be covered by small squares that each grow by k². The circle of lesson 6 is an example, since its area, πr², grows with the square of its radius.

lead.text: The area factor lets you find the area of a copy without measuring it again. A plot of land has an area of 40 m², and a similar plot with every length multiplied by 6 has an area factor of 6² = 36, so its area is 40 × 36 = 1440 m².

afterFigure.text: The rule works for *reductions* as well. If every length of the original plot is halved, the area factor is ½ × ½ = ¼, and the area falls to 40 ÷ 4 = 10 m². **Square the length factor first, then multiply the area by the result.** Multiplying the area by the length factor itself is the commonest slip, and it gives 240 m² for the enlarged plot, a sixth of the true value.

lead.text: The rule can be turned round when the areas are known. If a similar copy has 64 times the area of the original, the length factor *k* satisfies k × k = 64, and the number that multiplies by itself to give 64 is 8, so every length has been multiplied by 8.

afterFigure.text: The number that multiplies by itself to give another is its **square root**, written √, so √64 = 8 and √144 = 12. **Square to go from lengths to area, and take the square root to go back**, and check the result by squaring it, since 8 × 8 = 64.

lessons.orientation: Distinguish a length scale factor from the resulting area factor.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Paint is sold by the area it covers, and a wall that is twice as wide and twice as high as another, with every length multiplied by 2, does not need twice as much paint. Expecting twice as much treats area as though it were a length, but an area depends on two lengths at once, so when both grow it grows by more than a factor of 2.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to find the area of a similar copy from its length scale factor, and work back from an area to the factor.

recap.keyIdea: When every length is multiplied by a scale factor k, the area is multiplied by k × k, so the area factor is the square of the length factor.

blocks.text: Enlarging a shape by a scale factor multiplies its width and its height each by that factor, so its area is multiplied by the factor twice over: a scale factor of 3 gives an area nine times as large, and a factor of one half gives a quarter of the area.

To go back from an area factor to the length factor, take its square root. The squared factor applies only when every length is multiplied, since a change to one length alone multiplies the area once by that change.

recap.nextHook: So far lengths have been measured or scaled; the next lesson gives a rule that finds the third side of a right triangle from the other two.

lessons.title: Right-triangle distances

lead.text: A triangle with a right angle has two special kinds of side. The two sides that meet at the right angle are its **legs**, and the third side, which lies opposite the right angle and is always the *longest*, is its **hypotenuse**. The figure shows two right triangles with their legs measured and the hypotenuse marked with a question mark.

afterFigure.text: Going from one end of the hypotenuse to the other by way of the legs means walking the full length of each, so that route is the sum of the two measurements: 2 + 5 = 7 in the first triangle and 4 + 6 = 10 in the second. The hypotenuse is the straight line between the same two ends, and the question for this lesson is how long it is when only the legs are known.

lead.text: The length of the hypotenuse follows from the legs by a rule about squares. Draw a square on each side of a right triangle, with that side as one of its edges, and the area of each square is the square of its side.

afterFigure.text: The square on the leg of length 3 has area 3 × 3 = 9 and the square on the leg of length 4 has area 4 × 4 = 16. Together they make 25, which is the area of the square on the hypotenuse, so the hypotenuse is 5, because 5 × 5 = 25. This is **Pythagoras' theorem**: **in a right triangle the squares on the two legs together have the same area as the square on the hypotenuse**. Writing a and b for the legs and c for the hypotenuse, it says:

To get from c² to c you take the [[square root|The number that multiplies by itself to give a number, as 6 does for 36. Met in “When area scales”.]], so legs of 4 and 6 give 16 + 36 = 52 and a hypotenuse of √52, which is about 7.2.

lead.text: The rule uses the hypotenuse in one particular place, so the first step in any problem is to find it. It is the side opposite the right angle and the longest side, and in a diagram the right angle carries a small square, so the side facing that square is the hypotenuse.

afterFigure.text: Take a right triangle with legs of 9 and 40 centimetres. The legs are squared and added, 9² + 40² = 81 + 1600 = 1681, and the hypotenuse is the square root of that, √1681 = 41 centimetres. **Square, add, then take the root**: adding the legs directly gives 49, and stopping before the root gives 1681, and both are wrong. The rule also needs a right angle. In a triangle without one, the squares on the two shorter sides *do not* add up to the square on the longest, so look for the marker before using it.

lead.text: When the hypotenuse is known and a leg is missing, the rule is used the *other* way round. Since a² + b² = c², the missing leg satisfies b² = c² − a², so you subtract the square of the known leg from the square of the hypotenuse and take the root.

afterFigure.text: Take the same triangle with a hypotenuse of 41 and one leg of 9. Then b² = 41² − 9² = 1681 − 81 = 1600, and b = √1600 = 40. **The hypotenuse is the square that the legs are added to, so a leg is found by subtracting.** The hypotenuse must come out longer than either leg, and a missing leg that comes out longer than the hypotenuse is a sign that the subtraction has been done the wrong way round.

lessons.orientation: Find a missing side using squared lengths and identify when the Pythagorean theorem applies.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: In a right triangle, squares drawn on the two shorter sides together cover exactly as much area as the square drawn on the longest side. This is **Pythagoras' theorem**, and it gives the length of the longest side from the other two, with nothing to measure along it.
The relation also runs backwards: when the longest side and one shorter side are known, the square on the missing side is what remains of the large square once the other small square is taken away.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to find the hypotenuse of a right triangle from its legs, and a missing leg from the hypotenuse and the other leg.

recap.keyIdea: In a right triangle the squares on the two legs add up to the square on the hypotenuse, a² + b² = c², which finds any one side from the other two.

blocks.text: The hypotenuse is the side opposite the right angle and the longest side, and its length is the square root of the sum of the squares of the legs, so legs of 3 and 4 give √25 = 5. To find a leg instead, subtract the square of the known leg from the square of the hypotenuse and take the root.
The rule holds only when the triangle has a right angle, and it always works with squares: adding the lengths themselves, or forgetting the final square root, gives a wrong answer.

recap.nextHook: A right triangle is hidden between any two points on a grid, and the next lesson uses the rule to find the straight-line distance between them from their coordinates.

lessons.title: Distance on a grid

lead.text: A point on a grid is described by two numbers, its **coordinates**, written (x, y): x says how far the point lies to the right of the starting point, or to the left if it is negative, and y says how far up, or down if it is negative. The figure shows two pairs of points, A and B, and the route between them that keeps to the grid lines, going *across* first and then *up*.

afterFigure.text: Along that route the first part changes only x and the second part changes only y, so each part is found by subtracting. In the first view A is at (2, 1) and B at (8, 4), so the route goes across by 8 − 2 = 6 and up by 4 − 1 = 3. These are the two **coordinate differences**, and the route along the grid lines, called the **grid path**, has length 6 + 3 = 9.

lead.text: The straight line from A to B is shorter than the grid path, and it can be found because the path has a right angle in it. The across part and the up part meet at a right angle, so they are the legs of a right triangle and the straight line is its [[hypotenuse|The longest side of a right triangle, opposite the right angle. Met in “Right-triangle distances”.]]. By [[Pythagoras' theorem|In a right triangle the squares on the two legs add up to the square on the hypotenuse. Met in “Right-triangle distances”.]] its length is the square root of the sum of the squares of the two coordinate differences.

afterFigure.text: Take A at (−2, −3) and B at (7, 9) in the figure. The differences are 7 − (−2) = 9 across and 9 − (−3) = 12 up, so the squares are 81 and 144, which add to 225, and the straight-line distance is √225 = 15 units, against a grid path of 9 + 12 = 21. **The grid path adds the differences; the straight line squares them, adds the squares and takes the root.** Writing a position as a pair of numbers goes back to René Descartes, whose *La Géométrie* of 1637 joined algebra to geometry, and the pairs are called Cartesian coordinates in his honour.

lead.text: Subtract the starting coordinate from the finishing one, and remember that subtracting a negative number *adds* it. A point at x = −5 and another at x = 3 are 3 − (−5) = 8 units apart, which is the 5 units from −5 to zero together with the 3 units from zero to 3.

afterFigure.text: Now take A at (−5, −6) and B at (3, 9). The differences are 3 − (−5) = 8 across and 9 − (−6) = 15 up, so the distance is √(8² + 15²) = √(64 + 225) = √289 = 17 units. It does not matter which point is taken first, because reversing the subtraction only changes the sign of a difference and squaring removes the sign, so (−8)² = 64, the same as 8². **Subtract the same way for both coordinates, square, add, and take the root.**

lead.text: Sliding a segment to a new place without *turning* it is called a **translation**: every point moves by the same amount. The segment from (0, 0) to (3, 4) has differences 3 and 4, so its length is √(9 + 16) = 5, and sliding it 6 units right and 2 units down puts its ends at (6, −2) and (9, 2).

afterFigure.text: The new differences are 9 − 6 = 3 across and 2 − (−2) = 4 up, the same as before, so the length is again 5. **A difference does not change when the same amount is added to both numbers**, since (x₂ + 6) − (x₁ + 6) is just x₂ − x₁. The distance formula uses only differences, so it cannot tell where on the grid a segment lies, but only how far apart its ends are.

lessons.orientation: Use coordinate differences as right-triangle legs and distinguish direct distance from a grid path.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A position on a map or a plan can be given by two numbers, how far along and how far up from a chosen starting point, and the straight-line distance between two such positions can be calculated from the four numbers alone, with no ruler. The calculation uses Pythagoras' theorem again, applied to the gap across and the gap up between the two positions.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to find the straight-line distance between two points from their coordinates, and tell it apart from the length of a grid path.

recap.keyIdea: The straight-line distance between two points is the square root of the squared coordinate differences added together, while the grid path just adds the differences.

blocks.text: The coordinate differences between two points are the legs of a right triangle, so the straight-line distance between them is √(dx² + dy²), where dx and dy are found by subtracting one point's coordinates from the other's. The grid path, which keeps to the lines, is the longer sum dx + dy.
Negative coordinates are handled by the same subtraction, and since only differences matter, moving a whole segment without turning it leaves its length unchanged.

recap.nextHook: Lengths and areas lie in a flat plane; the next lesson adds a third dimension and measures the space inside a box.

lessons.title: Filling space

lead.text: To measure how much space a box holds, fill it with **unit cubes**, cubes whose edges are one unit long, and count them. The box in the figure is 6 units long, 3 units wide and 2 units high, and the cubes can be packed in flat layers, one on top of another.

afterFigure.text: The bottom layer covers the base of the box, which is 6 by 3, so it holds 6 × 3 = 18 cubes, exactly as many as the base has [[unit squares|Squares whose sides are one unit long, used to measure area. Met in “Boundary and area”.]]. The box is 2 units high, so it has *two* such layers and holds 18 × 2 = 36 cubes. This count is the **volume** of the box. **The volume of a box is its length times its width times its height**, because the base gives the cubes in one layer and the height gives the number of layers.

lead.text: Volume is measured in cubic units, in the same way that area is measured in square units. A cube whose edges are 1 centimetre long has a volume of one **cubic centimetre**, written 1 cm³, so a box that holds 36 of those cubes has a volume of 36 cm³.

afterFigure.text: A length such as an edge is in centimetres, an area such as the base is in square centimetres, cm², and a volume is in cubic centimetres, cm³, with *one more* factor of length for each extra dimension. A cube 10 cm on each edge holds 10 × 10 × 10 = 1000 cm³, which is exactly one litre, so a litre of water just fills a box of that size.

lead.text: A box has three edge lengths, and nothing in the calculation depends on *which* face it stands on.

afterFigure.text: Lying down, the box is 9 long, 2 wide and 3 high, so its **base area** is 9 × 2 = 18 and its volume is 18 × 3 = 54. Standing on its end, the base is 3 by 2, with an area of 6, and the height is 9, so the volume is 6 × 9 = 54 as well. **Volume is the base area multiplied by the height**, and since multiplication can be done in any order the result is the same for every choice of base.

steps.headline: A 4 by 3 base, five units high

workedSteps.text: The base is 4 by 3, so one layer holds this many cubes.
The box is 5 layers high. How many cubes does it hold in all?

lead.text: The rule can be run backwards to find a missing edge. Since volume is base area times height, the height is the volume *divided by* the base area. The figure shows two boxes with the same 7 by 2 base and their volumes.

afterFigure.text: The base area is 7 × 2 = 14. The first box holds 56 cm³, so its height is 56 ÷ 14 = 4 cm. **Divide the volume by the base area to find the height**, and check by multiplying back, since 14 × 4 = 56.

lead.text: A cube has three equal edges, so its volume is three copies of the edge multiplied together.

afterFigure.text: The cube with an edge of 2 holds 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 unit cubes, and the cube with an edge of 3 holds 3 × 3 × 3 = 27. **The volume of a cube is its edge length multiplied by itself three times**, written s³ and read 's cubed', just as s² is read 's squared' for the area of a square.

lessons.orientation: Count volume in cubic units, then work back from a volume to a missing height.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: How much a box holds, whether it is a fish tank full of water or a shipping container full of cargo, is found in the same way as an area, by choosing a small standard piece and counting how many of them fit.
For a flat shape the standard piece was a square, but a box has a third direction, so the piece must be a cube, and counting how many fit turns out to need only the three edge lengths of the box.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to find the volume of a box in cubic units, and work back from a volume to a missing height.

recap.keyIdea: The volume of a box is its base area times its height, which is length × width × height, measured in cubic units.

blocks.text: A box fills with layers of unit cubes, each layer as large as the base and as many layers as the height, so its volume is the base area times the height. A cube's volume is its edge multiplied by itself three times, and the answer is in cubic units such as cm³.
Because the rule is a product, it can be run backwards: dividing the volume by the base area gives the height.

recap.nextHook: A box also has a surface, and the next lesson unfolds it flat to find how much material it takes to cover it.

lessons.title: Unfolding surface area

lead.text: The flat sides of a box are its **faces**, and each one is a rectangle. If you cut along some of its edges and fold the sides out flat, the box becomes a single piece called its **net**, and the *Unfold box* button in the figure does exactly this.

afterFigure.text: The net is the covering of the box laid flat, so the paper needed to wrap the box is the total area of its faces. That total is the box's **surface area**. **To find a surface area, find the area of every face and add them**, and the net is a way of making sure that none is missed or counted twice.

lead.text: A cube is the simplest box to cover, because all its faces are the *same* square. A cube with an edge of 2 has faces of 2 × 2 = 4 square units, and with six of them its surface area is 6 × 4 = 24 square units.

afterFigure.text: **The surface area of a cube is six times the square of its edge**, and it is measured in square units, because it adds up areas. The cube with an edge of 2 also has a [[volume|The number of unit cubes that fill a solid. Met in “Filling space”.]] of 8 cubic units, which is a different quantity with a different unit.

lead.text: Opposite faces are *equal*, so a net always shows three matching pairs: the top and base, the front and back, and the two ends. The figure shows a pencil case 10 long, 4 wide and 3 high.

afterFigure.text: For the pencil case the top and base are each 10 × 4 = 40, the front and back are 10 × 3 = 30 each, and the two ends are 4 × 3 = 12 each, so the three different face areas are 40, 30 and 12. They add to 82, and doubling counts both faces of each pair, giving 2 × 82 = 164 square units. **Add the three different face areas, then double**, which for a box of length l, width w and height h is written:

steps.headline: The surface area of a 5 by 3 by 2 box

workedSteps.text: The three different faces have these areas.
Each of the three has a matching face opposite it. What is the total surface area?

lead.text: An open box such as a tray or a skip has a face missing, and its covering is the closed total less that face. Removing a lid takes away exactly *one* face and leaves the other five untouched.

afterFigure.text: A closed box 4 by 3 by 2 has faces of 12, 8 and 6, so its surface area is 2 × 26 = 52 square units. If its top, which measures 4 by 3 and so has an area of 12, is left off, the covering is 52 − 12 = 40 square units. **Find the closed total first, then subtract the one face that is missing.**

lead.text: The box in the figure measures 2 by 1 by 1, with faces of 2, 2 and 1, so its surface area is 2 × (2 + 2 + 1) = 10 square units and its volume is 2 × 1 × 1 = 2 cubic units. The second view triples every length.

afterFigure.text: The tripled box is 6 by 3 by 3, with faces of 18, 18 and 9, so its surface area is 2 × (18 + 18 + 9) = 90, which is 9 times as much, and its volume is 6 × 3 × 3 = 54, which is 27 times as much. **Surface area grows by the square of the scale factor and volume by its cube**, since an area contains two lengths and a volume three, and 3² = 9 while 3³ = 27. Galileo drew the same conclusion for living things in his *Two New Sciences* of 1638, arguing that a larger animal needs disproportionately thick bones, because its weight grows with its volume while the strength of a bone grows only with its cross-section.

lessons.orientation: Unfold a box to find the paper it needs, and see how that amount grows with the box.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A cardboard box cut along some of its edges and pressed flat becomes a single piece of card made of rectangles joined edge to edge. That piece is the same material that covered the box, so its area is the amount of paper or paint that the outside of the box needs.
Unfolding turns a calculation on a solid into a sum of rectangle areas.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to find the surface area of a box from its net, and say how surface area and volume grow when the box is enlarged.

recap.keyIdea: The surface area of a box is twice the sum of its three different face areas, and when every length is multiplied by k the surface area is multiplied by k² and the volume by k³.

blocks.text: Unfolding a box into its net shows its faces in three equal pairs, so its surface area is twice the sum of the three different face areas, and a box with a missing lid loses one face's area from that total.

When every length is multiplied by a scale factor, each face grows by the factor squared and the volume by the factor cubed, which is why the material that covers a solid and the space inside it grow at different rates.

questions.prompt: A 90° corner contains a 35° angle. How many degrees remain?
hints: Identify the total turn of the corner.
Subtract the known part from the total.
Calculate 90 − 35.
questions.onCorrect: The two parts fill the corner, so they add to 90°. Take the part you know from the whole.

misconceptions.feedback: 35° is the part you were given. The question asks for the part that is left.
That adds the 35° to the corner. The two parts together make the corner, not more.

questions.prompt: Two angles sit side by side on a straight line. One is 68°. What is the other, in degrees?
hints: A straight line represents a half-turn.
The adjacent angles add to 180°.
Calculate 180 − 68.
questions.onCorrect: The other angle is 180° − 68° = 112°: the two angles fill the half-turn.

misconceptions.feedback: 68° is the angle you were given. Find the part that is left.
That adds 180 to 68. The whole is 180°, so the other part is smaller than that.

questions.prompt: A pointer has turned 140°. How many more degrees complete a full 360° turn in the same direction?
hints: Use a full turn as the total.
Find the turn that has not yet been made.
Calculate 360 − 140.
questions.onCorrect: 220°. The turn so far and the turn left make a full 360°.

misconceptions.feedback: 140° is the turn already made. The question asks for the part still to come.
That is 180 − 140. A whole turn is 360°, not 180°.

questions.prompt: The arms of an angle are drawn twice as long, along the same lines. What happens to its size in degrees?
hints: Separate the length of a ray from its direction.

acceptedIdeas: It stays the same
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The degree measure depends on the directions of the rays, so extending them leaves the angle unchanged.

choices.label: It doubles
It is halved
It stays the same

questions.onCorrect: The angle stays the same. It measures how far you turn, not how long the arms are.

misconceptions.feedback: A longer arm covers more paper, not more turn. The directions of the arms haven't changed.
Nothing was cut. The arms point the same way, so the turn is the same.

questions.prompt: A right angle is split into 27° and another angle. Find the other angle in degrees.
hints: A right angle is the whole.
Subtract the part already given.
Calculate 90 − 27.
questions.onCorrect: 63°. The parts of a right angle add to 90°, so subtract the part you know.

misconceptions.feedback: 117° comes from starting at 180°. A right angle is a quarter-turn, so start from 90°.
27° is the part you were given. Find the other part.

questions.prompt: Which pair of angles can sit side by side to form a straight angle?
hints: Add each pair and compare with a half-turn.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 72° + 108° = 180°, the measure of a straight angle.

questions.onCorrect: 72° + 108° = 180°. Two angles on a straight line fill a half-turn.

misconceptions.feedback: Those add to 90°, a right angle. A straight angle is a half-turn.
Those add to more than a half-turn: 190°.

questions.prompt: A triangle has angles 48° and 67°. What is its third angle in degrees?
hints: All three angles of a triangle together make 180°.
Add the two angles you are given.
Subtract 48 + 67 from 180.
questions.onCorrect: 65°. Take the two angles you know from 180°.

misconceptions.feedback: That's the two angles added. The third angle is what is left of 180°.
That leaves out the 67° angle. All three angles share the total.

questions.prompt: A right triangle has another angle of 32°. Find its third angle in degrees.
hints: The right angle uses half of the triangle's total.
The two acute angles add to 90°.
Calculate 90 − 32.
questions.onCorrect: 58°. The right angle and the 32° use 122° of the 180°, and the two acute angles share 90°.

misconceptions.feedback: 90° is the right angle you already have. Find the third angle.
That leaves out the right angle. Take it from 180° as well.

questions.prompt: A triangle has two equal angles and a third angle of 44°. Find one of the equal angles in degrees.
hints: Take the unequal angle from 180°.
Split what remains equally between two angles.
Halve the leftover.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The equal angles share 180 − 44 = 136°; each is 136/2 = 68°.

questions.onCorrect: 68°. The two equal angles share what the third leaves, so halve it.

misconceptions.feedback: 136° is what the two equal angles share. Each gets half of it.
44° is the third angle, which you were given. Find the equal pair.

questions.prompt: Can a triangle have two right angles?
hints: Add up what two right angles use.

acceptedIdeas: No, the third angle would have nothing left.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No, the third angle would have nothing left.

choices.label: Yes, if its sides are long enough.
No, the third angle would have nothing left.
Yes, if its third angle is also 90°.

questions.onCorrect: No. Two right angles use all 180°, so there is nothing left for a third angle.

misconceptions.feedback: Side length doesn't change the total. The three angles of any triangle add to 180°.
Three right angles would add to 270°, far past 180°.

questions.prompt: A triangular sign has angles 39° and 86°. Find its third angle in degrees.
hints: Treat all three angles as parts of 180°.
Find the total of the two given angles.
Calculate 180 − (39 + 86).
questions.onCorrect: 55°. Whatever the shape, the other two angles leave 180° minus their sum.

misconceptions.feedback: That's 39 + 86. The third angle is what is left of 180°.
That leaves out the 86° angle. Take both known angles from 180°.

questions.prompt: Which set can be the three angles of a triangle?
hints: Check both the total and whether every angle is positive.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 40° + 60° + 80° = 180° and all three measures are positive.

questions.onCorrect: 40° + 60° + 80° = 180°. A triangle's angles must add to exactly 180°.

misconceptions.feedback: Those add to 210°, which is too much.
Those add to 190°, which is too much.

questions.prompt: Rectangle A is 6 m by 4 m and rectangle B is 8 m by 2 m. Which statement is true?
hints: Add the sides round each rectangle.
Count the rows of squares in each, then the squares per row.
Compare the two boundary totals, then the two square counts.

acceptedIdeas: They have the same perimeter but different areas
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Both perimeters are 20, while their areas are 24 and 16 square units.

choices.label: They have the same perimeter but different areas
They have the same area but different perimeters
They have equal areas and equal perimeters

questions.onCorrect: Equal perimeters can hide different areas. Add the sides for one, count squares for the other.

misconceptions.feedback: Add the four sides of each rectangle. Do the two totals really differ?
Count the squares in each rectangle. Do they hold the same number?

questions.prompt: Find the perimeter of a rectangle 6 units long and 4 units wide.
hints: Perimeter is the total boundary.
There are two sides of each length.
Calculate 2 × (6 + 4).
questions.onCorrect: Perimeter adds all four sides. Opposite sides are equal, so two of each length.

misconceptions.feedback: That's 6 × 4, the area. Perimeter is the distance round the edge.
That's 6 + 4, only half the boundary. Count all four sides.

questions.prompt: Find the area of a rectangle 6 units long and 4 units wide, in square units.
hints: Count square units inside the boundary.
Use the number of rows and squares in each row.
Multiply 6 by 4.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Six squares per row across four rows give 6 × 4 = 24 square units.

questions.onCorrect: Area counts squares inside: 4 rows of 6, so 6 × 4, in square units.

misconceptions.feedback: That's the distance round the edge. Area counts the squares inside.
That adds 6 + 4. Area multiplies rows by squares in each row.

questions.prompt: A rectangle is 7 units by 3 units. What area does it cover in square units?
hints: Area counts the inside.
Multiply the two perpendicular dimensions.
Calculate 7 × 3.
questions.onCorrect: 21 square units. Rows times squares per row gives the area of any rectangle.

misconceptions.feedback: That's the distance round the edge. Area counts the squares inside.
That adds 7 + 3. Area multiplies the two sides.

questions.prompt: A rectangular floor has area 54 m² and width 6 m. Find its length in metres.

Undo multiplication by the known width.
Divide 54 by 6.

Square metres
Cubic metres
